title: Leviathan: Decoupling Input and Output Representations in Language Models
claim: A compact index-to-embedding module, replicated and summed as input to a standard Transformer, replaces the input embedding matrix.
layout: 2 vertical block-diagram panels, bottom-to-top flow, left module zoomed into right architecture
description: Two side-by-side vertical block diagrams, both flowing bottom to top with thick black arrows. The left panel shows the LEV head. A token ID i fans out into three indices i1, i2, i3. Each goes through a tall rotated 'Encode' box, then a Dense layer, a Layer Norm and a Spline Basis block. The three branches merge into a Product block, then a final Dense layer, ending at 'Head Contribution'. The right panel shows the full Leviathan model. A Token goes into an 'LEV Head' box marked ×h, then a Sum block. That feeds a grey rounded box marked ×L, which holds a standard Transformer block: LayerNorm, Attention, LayerNorm, Dense and two residual skip arrows. The output goes through Layer Norm and Dense to 'Next Token'. Pastel fills mark layer types: pink for embedding, blue for Dense, orange for norm, green for attention and product, purple for spline.
caption: Left, LEV head: maps token index $i$ to an embedding via compositional base-$b$ encoding, a learned seed projection, separable B-spline basis expansion and rank-$r$ tensor product. Right, The full Leviathan architecture. $h$ LEV heads are summed to produce the input embedding, which is fed into a standard $L$-layer decoder-only Transformer.
abstract: Modern language models use a single matrix for input embedding and output projection. This couples two distinct objectives: token representation and discrimination over a vocabulary. This work introduces Leviathan, a Transformer architecture that replaces the input embedding matrix with learned embedding vectorization (LEV), a compact continuous mapping from token indices to embeddings. Leviathan's output head remains untied for a parameter increase of as low as 0.2%. Under controlled comparisons with identical Transformer backbones, Leviathan consistently improves language modeling performance over standard tied-embedding baselines across a 200M-1.2B parameter regime on The Pile with gains that grow during training. At 1.2B scale, Leviathan reduces validation perplexity by 9%, requires $2.1\times$ fewer training tokens to reach the tied baseline's final loss, and improves on all six downstream benchmarks evaluated, including a 30% reduction in LAMBADA perplexity. Frequency-stratified analysis reveals gains to be concentrated in rare tokens, where continuous parameterization reduces perplexity by 81%, falling to near zero for the most frequent.
